rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعطاء وعكرمة
rows.claim: Success is attaining Paradise by purifying oneself from shirk through faith.
rows.anchor: من تطهر من الشرك بإيمان قاله ابن عباس وعطاء وعكرمة

rows.speaker: الحسن والربيع
rows.claim: They interpret purification as one's deeds being wholesome and growing in reward.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن والربيع: من كان عمله زاكيا ناميا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He explains purification as performing a righteous deed.
rows.anchor: وقال معمر عن قتادة: «تزكى» قام بعمل صالح

rows.speaker: قتادة وعطاء وأبو العالية
rows.claim: They say the verse was revealed concerning the charity of breaking the fast.
rows.anchor: وعنه وعن عطاء وأبي العالية: نزلت في صدقة الفطر

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: He says the person gave charity and then went out to pray.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن سيرين { قد أفلح من تزكى * وذكر اسم ربه فصلى }. قال

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: He describes a man saying that he would put his zakat before his prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: كان الرجل يقول أقدم زكاتي بين يدي صلاتي

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري وابن عمر وأبو العالية
rows.claim: They identify the acts as fitr charity and the Eid prayer; Abu al-Aliya says people of Medina rank it among the best charities, alongside giving water.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي سعيد الخدري وابن عمر: أن ذلك في صدقة الفطر، وصلاة العيد

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report through Kathir ibn Abd Allah says purification means paying zakat al-fitr and remembering God then praying means the Eid prayer.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله تعالى: { قد أفلح من تزكى } قال:«أخرج زكاة الفطر»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: They interpret remembering the Lord as saying His name on the way to the prayer ground, followed by the Eid prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس والضحاك: { وذكر اسم ربه } في طريق المصلى

rows.speaker: أبو الأحوص وعطاء
rows.claim: They take purification to mean payment of all obligatory wealth zakat.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالآية زكاة الأموال كلها قاله أبو الأحوص وعطاء

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: In Ibn Jurayj's report, Ata says the verse concerns all charitable giving, not only fitr charity.
rows.anchor: قلت لعطاء: { قد أفلح من تزكى } للفطر؟ قال: هي للصدقات كلها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is purification of one's deeds from ostentation and shortcomings; the wording is apt because wealth is more often described with zakā than tazakkā.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي زكاة الأعمال، لا زكاة الأموال

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Jabir explains purification as confessing God's oneness, rejecting idols, and affirming Muhammad's messengership.
rows.anchor: وروى جابر بن عبد الله قال: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He glosses tazakkā as the confession that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس { تزكى } قال: لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: He reports its revelation about Uthman, who gave an orchard to replace a hypocrite's palm whose fallen dates fed an Ansari family; the hypocrite had refused the Prophet's offer of a palm in Paradise.
rows.anchor: وروى عنه عطاء قال: " نزلت في عثمان بن عفان رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding warning that the most wretched will avoid the reminder is also said to have been revealed about a hypocrite.
rows.anchor: ونزلت في المنافق { ويتجنبها الأشقى }

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He says the verses were revealed about Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.
rows.anchor: وذكر الضحاك أنها نزلت في أبي بكر الصديق رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the majority regard the surah as Meccan, Mecca had neither Eid nor fitr zakat; al-Qushayri says the praise may anticipate future obedience to those commands.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم أن هذه السورة مكية في قول الجمهور، ولم يكن بمكة عيد

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Remembering God recalls the return and standing before Him, leading one to worship and pray.
rows.anchor: وروى عطاء عن ابن عباس قال: يرد ذكر معاده وموقفه بين يدي الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God's name is the opening takbir; this supports its obligation and its being outside the prayer, since prayer is coordinated after it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ذكر اسم ربه بالتكبير في أول الصلاة، لأنها لا تنعقد إلا بذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same proof is used for permitting the opening takbir with any of God's names, a disputed issue among jurists.
rows.anchor: وفيه حجة لمن قال: إن الافتتاح جائز بكل اسم من أسماء الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He interprets the remembrance on the way to the prayer ground and the prayer as the Eid takbirs and Eid prayer.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: «وذكر اسم ربه» في طريق المصلى «فصلى» أي صلاة العيد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Remembrance may be inward during prayer, prompting fear of punishment and hope for reward, and thus complete observance and humility.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { وذكر اسم ربه } وهو أن يذكره بقلبه عند صلاته

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading takes the remembrance as beginning each surah with the basmala; prayer and remembrance need not occur in the stated order.
rows.anchor: هو أن يفتتح أول كل سورة ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction does not require chronology, as in saying either that someone honored then visited me or visited then honored me.
rows.anchor: ولا فرق بين أن تقول: أكرمتني فزرتني، وبين أن تقول: زرتني فأكرمتني

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the prayer as the five obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هذا في الصلاة المفروضة، وهي الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Prayer may mean supplication to God for worldly and afterlife needs.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الدعاء أي دعاء الله بحوائج الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري وابن عمر
rows.claim: They also identify the prayer as the Eid prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل: صلاة العيد قاله أبو سعيد الخدري وابن عمر وغيرهما

rows.speaker: أبو الأحوص
rows.claim: He understands the prayer as voluntary prayer after paying zakat; this also follows from Ata's interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو أن يتطوع بصلاة بعد زكاته قاله أبو الأحوص

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: He says that one who performs prayer but does not pay zakat has no prayer.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عبد الله قال: من أقام الصلاة ولم يؤت الزكاة فلا صلاة له

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ونصر بن عاصم
rows.claim: They read the verb in the third person, supplying ‘the most wretched’ as its subject; the common second-person reading is supported by Ubayy's ‘rather, you prefer.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو ونصر بن عاصم «بل يؤثرون» بالياء على الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the common second-person reading, the address says that people prefer worldly abundance over abundance of reward.
rows.anchor: وعلى الأول فيكون تأويلها بل تؤثرون أيها المسلمون الاستكثار من الدنيا، للاستكثار من الثواب

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: He explains that people chose the present world because its pleasures and food arrived quickly, while the afterlife was unseen, so they took the near and left the deferred.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود أنه قرأ هذه الآية، فقال: أتدرون لم آثرنا الحياة الدنيا على الآخرة؟

rows.speaker: أبو موسى
rows.claim: He urges Anas to spend time remembering God after people nearly tear one another apart with talk of worldly matters.
rows.anchor: وروى ثابت عن أنس قال: كنا مع أبي موسى في مسير، والناس يتكلمون

rows.speaker: أبو موسى
rows.claim: He says the world was hastened and the afterlife hidden; if people saw it, they would never turn away or prefer anything to it.
rows.anchor: ثم قال: يا أنس، ما ثبر الناس! ما بطأ بهم؟ قلت: الدنيا والشيطان والشهوات. قال: لا، ولكن عجلت الدنيا، وغيبت الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife means Paradise; it is better and more enduring than this world.
rows.anchor: أي والدار الآخرة أي الجنة. { خير } أي أفضل. { وأبقى } أي أدوم من الدنيا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A hadith likens this world against the afterlife to the water a finger brings back from the sea; Qurtubi marks it authentic.
rows.anchor: ما الدنيا في الآخرة إلا كما يضع أحدكم أصبعه في اليم، فلينظر بم يرجع

rows.speaker: مالك بن دينار
rows.claim: Even if this world were perishable gold and the afterlife lasting pottery, one should choose the latter; in reality their relative worth is the reverse.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك بن دينار: لو كانت الدنيا من ذهب يفنى، والآخرة من خزف يبقى، لكان الواجب

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: They identify ‘this’ as the teaching that the afterlife is better and more lasting, a truth reiterated throughout God's books.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة وابن زيد: يريد قوله: { والآخرة خير وأبقى }. وقالا: تتابعت كتب الله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He takes ‘this’ to mean all of God's scriptures.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: «إن هذا لفي الصحف الأولى» قال: كتب الله جل ثناؤه كلها

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He says the reference extends from ‘Successful is whoever purifies himself’ through the end of the surah, citing the report about Abu Dharr.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: { إن هذا لفي الصحف الأولى } من قوله: «قد أفلح» إلى آخر السورة

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies ‘this’ as the whole surah.
rows.anchor: وروى عكرمة عن ابن عباس: «إن هذا لفي الصحف الأولى» قال: هذه السورة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He interprets the reference as the Qur'an being present in the earlier scriptures.
rows.anchor: إن هذا القرآن لفي الصحف الأولى أي الكتب الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scrolls are revelations sent to Abraham and Moses; the claim is that their meaning occurs there, not that these exact words do.
rows.anchor: يعني الكتب المنزلة عليهما. ولم يرد أن هذه الألفاظ بعينها في تلك الصحف

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the report from Abu Dharr, Abraham's scrolls counsel a ruler against hoarding, urge justice even for a disbeliever, and prescribe reflection, self-accounting, livelihood, restraint, and purposeful speech.
rows.anchor: من حديث أبي ذر قال: قلت يا رسول الله، فما كانت صحف إبراهيم؟ قال: «كانت أمثالا كلها

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The same report says Moses' scrolls contain admonitions about death, destiny, worldly change, and working in view of the coming account.
rows.anchor: قال: قلت يا رسول الله، فما كانت صحف موسى؟ قال: «كانت عبرا كلها

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Asked whether any of Abraham's and Moses' teachings remain, he tells Abu Dharr to recite these concluding verses of al-Ala.
rows.anchor: قال: قلت يا رسول الله، فهل في أيدينا شيء مما كان في يدي إبراهيم وموسى

none: Continuation only says that the previously cited report continues; no new point.

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: He says ‘hal’ here means ‘already’ or ‘indeed,’ as in the opening of al-Insan.
rows.anchor: «هل» بمعنى قد كقوله: هل أتى على الإنسان

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: They identify the overwhelming event as the Resurrection, which covers creatures with terrors and dreadful scenes.
rows.anchor: أي القيامة التي تغشى الخلائق بأهوالها وأفزاعها قاله أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير ومحمد بن كعب
rows.claim: They identify the overwhelming event as the Fire covering the faces of disbelievers; Abu Salih transmits the view from Ibn Abbas, supported by 14:50.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير ومحمد بن كعب: «الغاشية»: النار تغشى وجوه الكفار

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations are that it covers all creatures, is the second blast for resurrection, or denotes the people who enter and cover themselves with Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تغشى الخلق. وقيل: المراد النفخة الثانية للبعث لأنها تغشى الخلائق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says this detailed account had not previously come to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لم يكن أتاه قبل ذلك على هذا التفصيل المذكور هاهنا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: The question is rhetorical: if the account had not reached the Prophet, it has now reached him.
rows.anchor: إن لم يكن أتاك حديث الغاشية فقد أتاك وهو معنى قول الكلبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says the Prophet had not known their account, so God informed him of it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لم يكن أتاه حديثهم، فأخبره عنهم

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: He glosses the faces as humbled by punishment; the word can denote anything diminished and still, and can describe humility in prayer or a lowered voice.
rows.anchor: { خاشعة } قال سفيان: أي ذليلة بالعذاب. وكل متضائل ساكن خاشع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Faces’ means the people who bear those faces.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالوجوه أصحاب الوجوه

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: They say the faces are in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة وابن زيد: «خاشعة» أي في النار

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: He says the faces belong to all disbelievers.
rows.anchor: والمراد وجوه الكفار كلهم قاله يحيى بن سلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from him narrows the faces to Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد وجوه اليهود والنصارى قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He first takes ‘toiling’ as a worldly state, since the afterlife is not an abode of action: they toil in this world and are humbled in the next.
rows.anchor: فهذا في الدنيا لأن الآخرة ليست دار عمل

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: The verb describes persistent effort, as with a man laboring through travel or a cloud whose lightning continues; a Hudhayli line illustrates the latter usage.
rows.anchor: يقال للرجل إذا دأب في سيره: قد عمل يعمل عملا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Nasiba’ means tired or exhausted.
rows.anchor: { ناصبة } أي تعبة. يقال: نصب بالكسر ينصب نصبا

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: They are idolaters, disbelieving scripturalists, monks, and others who exhausted themselves in sin and disbelief; God accepts only deeds done sincerely for Him.
rows.anchor: فروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس قال: هم الذين أنصبوا أنفسهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: They arrogantly refused God's obedience in life, then toil in Hell dragging heavy chains, bearing fetters, and standing barefoot and naked in a day lasting fifty thousand years.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد عن قتادة: «عاملة ناصبة» قال: تكبرت في الدنيا عن طاعة الله

rows.speaker: الحسن وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: They did not work or toil for God in life, so they will be made to work and toil in Hell.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وسعيد بن جبير: لم تعمل لله في الدنيا، ولم تنصب له

rows.speaker: الكلبي وابن عباس
rows.claim: They are dragged on their faces and may be forced up iron mountains, straining under chains and fetters and through fire.
rows.anchor: وعنه وعن غيره: يكلفون ارتقاء جبل من حديد في جهنم، فينصبون فيها

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن وعيسى وحميد
rows.claim: They read ‘nasiba’ in the accusative, either as a circumstantial accusative or as a term of censure; the rest read it nominative as an adjective or with an implied subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن وعيسى وحميد، ورواها عبيد عن شبل عن ابن كثير «ناصبة» بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If both descriptions apply in the afterlife, ‘toiling’ can be a second predicate of ‘faces’ and there is no pause at ‘humbled’; if the toil is worldly, the states may be divided across both lives.
rows.anchor: ومن جعل المعنى في الآخرة، جاز أن يكون خبرا بعد خبر عن «وجوه»

rows.speaker: عكرمة والسدي
rows.claim: They say the people performed sinful acts in this world.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة والسدي: عملت في الدنيا بالمعاصي

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: They identify the toiling people as monks living in cloisters; Ibn Abbas is also reported to hold this view.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير وزيد بن أسلم: هم الرهبان أصحاب الصوامع

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: When he saw an old, ragged monk in Syria, Umar wept and said the man had sought something without attaining it and hoped for something he missed, then recited these verses.
rows.anchor: هذا المسكين طلب أمرا فلم يصبه، ورجا رجاء فأخطأه، وقرأ قول الله

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: He defines taqahhul as shabby appearance, and a ragged, dry-skinned man as mutaqahhil.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي: التقهل: رثاثة الهيئة، ورجل متقهل: يابس الجلد

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: He defines taqahhul as complaining of need.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو: التقهل: شكوى الحاجة

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: He lists taqahhula as weakness and collapse, qahl as ingratitude for kindness or bad praise, and related forms for affected disgrace and self-defilement.
rows.anchor: والقهل: كفران الإحسان. وقد قهل يقهل قهلا: إذا أثنى ثناء قبيحا

rows.speaker: علي رضي الله عنه
rows.claim: He identifies the people described as the Haruriyya (Kharijites), whom the Prophet said would outdo others in visible prayer, fasting, and deeds yet leave the religion like an arrow through prey.
rows.anchor: وعن علي رضي الله عنه أنهم أهل حروراء يعني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire's heat reaches them; ‘hamiyah’ means intensely hot, heated and kept alight for a long time.
rows.anchor: { حامية } شديدة الحر أي قد أوقدت وأحميت المدة الطويلة

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: He records lexical forms for the height of daytime heat and the heat of the sun or oven.
rows.anchor: وحكى الكسائي: اشتد حمي الشمس وحموها: بمعنى

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وأبو بكر ويعقوب
rows.claim: They read ‘tasla’ with a prefixed damma; the others read it with fatha, and another reading doubles the consonant.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وأبو بكر ويعقوب «تصلى» بضم التاء. الباقون بفتحها

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Answering why fire is called hot, he offers four emphases: lasting heat, protection from violations like God's forbidden bounds, refusal of approach like a fierce lion, and the heat of rage and vengeance.
rows.anchor: الماوردي: فإن قيل فما معنى وصفها بالحمى، وهي لا تكون إلا حامية

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The second explanation invokes the hadith that every king has a protected domain and God's protected domain is His prohibitions; one who grazes nearby risks entering it.
rows.anchor: إن لكل ملك حمى، وإن حمى الله محارمه. ومن يرتع حول الحمى

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: His verse about wolves avoiding the charge of a fierce lion illustrates the fire's refusal to be approached or touched.
rows.anchor: وتتقي صولة المستأسد الحامي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Aniya’ describes heat brought to its limit; the word comes from a verb for delaying or keeping something back, and the same term appears for boiling water in 55:44.
rows.anchor: الآني: الذي قد انتهى حره من الإيناء، بمعنى التأخير

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Its heat has reached its limit; Hell has been kindled since creation, and the thirsty are driven to it.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: «آنية» أي حرها أدرك أوقدت عليها جهنم منذ خلقت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He says its heat has reached its utmost and the drink has become due.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد قال: بلغت أناها، وحان شربها

rows.speaker: التفاسير
rows.claim: Commentaries say a drop of this water would melt the mountains of this world.
rows.anchor: تناهى حرها فلو وقعت نقطة منها على جبال الدنيا لذابت

rows.speaker: عكرمة ومجاهد
rows.claim: They describe dhari as a thorny, ground-hugging plant called shibriq when fresh; when dry it is poisonous, foul, and avoided by animals. Qurtubi prefers the majority's view that it is a plant.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة ومجاهد: الضريع: نبت ذو شوك لاصق بالأرض

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says dhari is material thrown up by the sea and eaten by livestock, not people; camels that find it remain unsated and waste away.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الضحاك روى عن ابن عباس قال: هو شيء يرمي به البحر، يسمى الضريع

rows.speaker: أبو ذؤيب
rows.claim: His verse uses shibriq for fresh growth that dries into dhari, witnessing the plant interpretation.
rows.anchor: رعى الشبرق الريان حتى إذا ذوى وعاد ضريعا

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: His verse depicts camels held among dhari, illustrating the word in a description of poor grazing.
rows.anchor: وحبسن في هزم الضريع فكلها حدباء دامية اليدين حرود

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: He calls dhari a green plant with a foul smell, cast up by the sea.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل: الضريع: نبات أخضر منتن الريح، يرمي به البحر

rows.speaker: الوالبي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says it is a tree of fire that would burn the earth and everything on it if it existed here.
rows.anchor: وقال الوالبي عن ابن عباس: هو شجر من نار، ولو كانت في الدنيا لأحرقت الأرض

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وعكرمة
rows.claim: They identify dhari as stones.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: هو الحجارة، وقاله عكرمة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says Hell's dhari resembles thorns, is bitterer than aloe, fouler than carrion, and hotter than fire.
rows.anchor: الضريع: شيء يكون في النار، يشبه الشوك، أشد مرارة من الصبر

rows.speaker: المتوكل بن حمدان
rows.claim: He says he heard that the tree of Hell bears pus and blood and is bitterer than aloe; its eaters implore God for relief.
rows.anchor: سمعت المتوكل بن حمدان يسأل عن هذه الآية { ليس لهم طعام إلا من ضريع }

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He says dhari is among the punishments God has kept hidden.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هو بعض ما أخفاه الله من العذاب

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: He derives the name from the eater's humiliation and supplication to be excused from such loathsome, harsh food; al-Nahhas suggests a related derivation from ‘weak and lowly.’
rows.anchor: وقال ابن كيسان: هو طعام يضرعون عنده ويذلون، ويتضرعون منه إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Another report from him identifies dhari as zaqqum; an unattributed view says it is a valley in Hell.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أيضا: هو الزقوم. وقيل: هو واد في جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The food called dhari differs from the food called ghislin in 69:35–36; Hell has levels, with different people receiving dhari, ghislin, zaqqum, boiling water, or pus as food or drink.
rows.anchor: وقال هنا: «إلا من ضريع» وهو غير الغسلين.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He says dhari occupies a level containing nothing else, while zaqqum occupies another; alternatively, the verses describe different states, as in 55:44.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: الضريع في درجة ليس فيها غيره، والزقوم في درجة أخرى.

rows.speaker: القتبي
rows.claim: He allows that dhari and zaqqum could be plants of fire, or of a substance the fire does not consume; familiar names can refer to realities unlike their worldly counterparts.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الضريع وشجرة الزقوم نبتين من النار

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: He prefers the account that God preserves the plants in Hell to torment its inhabitants, just as He preserves them there.
rows.anchor: القشيري: وأمثل من قول القتبي أن نقول: إن الذي يبقي الكافرين في النار

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some claim dhari itself is not grown or eaten in Hell, but is a metaphor for food that fails to satisfy, like livestock fodder.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن الضريع بعينه لا ينبت في النار، ولا أنهم يأكلونه.

rows.speaker: الترمذي الحكيم
rows.claim: He calls that metaphorical explanation unsound and base, arguing it suggests doubt about God's power to grow a thorny plant in fire; green wood already yields fire without being consumed, as 36:80 says.
rows.anchor: قال الترمذي الحكيم: وهذا نظر سقيم من أهله وتأويل دنيء، كأنه يدل على أنهم تحيروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument that God can make the dead walk on their faces answers objections about unusual afterlife realities.
rows.anchor: الذي أمشاهم على أرجلهم قادر على أن يمشيهم على وجوههم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses likewise establish God's power to replace burned skin, clothe people in tar, and punish them with chains, fire, and choking food.
rows.anchor: كلما نضجت جلودهم بدلناهم جلودا غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's punishments take varied forms, including fetters, blazing fire, and food that catches in the throat.
rows.anchor: فإنما يتلون عليهم العذاب بهذه الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thorny food does not nourish or satisfy its eater.
rows.anchor: يعني الضريع لا يسمن آكله. وكيف يسمن من يأكل الشوك!

rows.speaker: المشركون
rows.claim: When the verse was revealed, they objected that their camels grew fat on dhari; Qurtubi says they were wrong because camels graze it fresh and do not eat it when dry.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: لما نزلت هذه الآية قال المشركون: إن إبلنا لتسمن بالضريع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: They may have mistaken dhari for other beneficial plants because of the similarity suggested by the word mudara'a, then found that it neither nourished nor relieved hunger.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اشتبه عليهم أمره فظنوه كغيره من النبت النافع، لأن المضارعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second set of faces belongs to believers, made joyful by seeing the outcome of their affairs and their good deeds.
rows.anchor: وهي وجوه المؤمنين نعمت بما عاينت من عاقبة أمرها وعملها الصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are pleased in the afterlife with the Paradise granted for their worldly effort; ‘pleased with their effort’ stands for pleased with its reward.
rows.anchor: { راضية } في الآخرة حين أعطيت الجنة بعملها. ومجازه: لثواب سعيها راضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unspoken conjunction separates this group of faces from the preceding group, and ‘faces’ stands for the souls.
rows.anchor: وفيها واو مضمرة. المعنى: ووجوه يومئذ، للفصل بينها وبين الوجوه المتقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden is high, either raised above the heavens as previously discussed or exalted in rank for its delights; its people abide there forever.
rows.anchor: { في جنة عالية } أي مرتفعة، لأنها فوق السموات حسب ما تقدم. وقيل: عالية القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden contains no worthless or unacceptable speech; laghiya, laghw, and lagha are equivalent terms, as a poetic line illustrates.
rows.anchor: أي كلاما ساقطا غير مرضي. وقال: { لاغية } ، واللغو واللغا واللاغية: بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He interprets the excluded speech as lies, slander, and disbelief in God.
rows.anchor: يعني كذبا وبهتانا وكفرا بالله عز وجل قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says there is no falsehood or sin there.
rows.anchor: لا باطل ولا إثم قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He identifies it as insulting speech.
rows.anchor: أنه الشتم قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He identifies it as disobedience.
rows.anchor: المعصية قاله الحسن

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He says no one there swears falsely; al-Kalbi broadens this to any oath, whether true or false.
rows.anchor: لا يسمع فيها حالف يحلف بكذب قاله الفراء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He also says the phrase excludes any idle word; Qurtubi prefers this broadest account, since Paradise's people speak only wisdom and praise God for lasting bliss.
rows.anchor: لا يسمع في كلامهم كلمة بلغو لأن أهل الجنة لا يتكلمون إلا بالحكمة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن كثير
rows.claim: They read the verb in the passive with a masculine ya; Nafi also reads it passive but with feminine ta because ‘laghiya’ is feminine.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وابن كثير «لا يسمع» بياء غير مسمى الفاعل

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: His passive feminine reading agrees the verb with the feminine noun; the other readers use active feminine ta, making the faces the subject that hear no idle speech.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه بالتاء المضمومة لأن اللاغية اسم مؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flowing spring pours freely, without channels, and supplies varied pleasant drinks; ‘spring’ can be a collective for the many springs mentioned in al-Insan.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { فيها عين جارية } أي بماء مندفق، وأنواع الأشربة اللذيذة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the raised couches stand as high as the distance between earth and sky so God's friend can view his surroundings.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه كان ارتفاعها قدر ما بين السماء والأرض، ليرى ولي الله ملكه حوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cups are placed ready; an ewer has a handle and spout, whereas a cup has neither.
rows.anchor: والكوب: إناء ليس له عروة ولا خرطوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cushions are arranged side by side; a poetic citation shows people seated on cushions and another records a cup passing among drinkers.
rows.anchor: { مصفوفة } أي واحدة إلى جنب الأخرى. قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: He records nummarqah as a small cushion, sometimes also the covering placed on a saddle.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح: النمرق والنمرقة: وسادة صغيرة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: He glosses zarabi as carpets.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: الزرابي: البسط

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He describes the carpets as fine-piled rugs.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الزرابي: الطنافس التي لها خمل رقيق

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says the carpets are spread out.
rows.anchor: والمبثوثة: المبسوطة قال قتادة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: He interprets the carpets as piled one on top of another.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بعضها فوق بعض قاله عكرمة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He says they are numerous.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كثيرة قاله الفراء

rows.speaker: القتبي
rows.claim: He says the carpets are dispersed through the sitting areas; Qurtubi calls this best, since it combines abundance with distribution.
rows.anchor: وقيل: متفرقة في المجالس قاله القتبي. قلت: هذا أصوب، فهي كثيرة متفرقة

rows.speaker: عمار بن محمد
rows.claim: He reports Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir reciting an added phrase, ‘reclining therein in comfort,’ after the carpet verse.
rows.anchor: قال حدثنا عمار بن محمد، قال: صليت خلف منصور بن المعتمر، فقرأ: { هل أتاك حديث الغاشية }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After disbelievers reject the two destinations, God recalls His creative power; camels come first because Arabs knew them, unlike elephants, and a small person can lead, kneel, raise, and load the great animal.
rows.anchor: تعجب الكفار من ذلك فكذبوا وأنكروا فذكرهم الله صنعته وقدرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Camels are land-ships: they endure long thirst, graze desert plants other beasts avoid, carry heavy loads, kneel for loading, then rise.
rows.anchor: صبرها على احتمال العطش حتى إن إظماءها ليرتفع إلى العشر فصاعدا

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل
rows.claim: They say the verse answers people wondering how they could climb elevated couches: as camels kneel to be loaded and then rise, the couches will lower and rise.
rows.anchor: قال معناه قتادة ومقاتل وغيرهما

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: He interprets the camels as great masses of clouds.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الإبل هنا القطع العظيمة من السحاب قاله المبرد

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: He transmits the cloud interpretation but says he found no basis for it in the recognized authorities' books.
rows.anchor: قال الثعلبي: وقيل في الإبل هنا: السحاب، ولم أجد لذلك ذلك أصلا في كتب الأئمة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: He distinguishes the light reading as the four-legged camel, which kneels to be loaded, from the heavy reading as rain-bearing clouds.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمرو: من قرأها «أفلا ينظرون إلى الإبل كيف خلقت» بالتخفيف: عنى به البعير

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: He presents livestock as the clearer, more famous meaning, though clouds are also possible; livestock gather food, drink, riding, and carrying uses in one animal, making their benefit and sign of power more complete.
rows.anchor: وقال الماوردي: وفي الإبل وجهان: أحدهما: وهو أظهرهما وأشهرهما: أنها الإبل من النعم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He says camels are singled out because they eat date stones and qat and produce milk.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: إنما خصها الله بالذكر لأنها تأكل النوى والقت، وتخرج اللبن

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Answering that elephants are more wondrous, he says Arabs were unfamiliar with them and they cannot be eaten, ridden, or milked.
rows.anchor: وسئل الحسن أيضا عنها وقالوا: الفيل أعظم في الأعجوبة: فقال: العرب بعيدة العهد بالفيل

rows.speaker: شريح
rows.claim: He would go out to the market area to contemplate how camels were created.
rows.anchor: وكان شريح يقول: اخرجوا بنا إلى الكناسة حتى ننظر إلى الإبل كيف خلقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun ibil has no singular from its own form and is feminine as a collective for nonhuman animals; its diminutive takes a feminine ending, and a lightened form and plural abal are also reported.
rows.anchor: والإبل: لا واحد لها من لفظها، وهي مؤنثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky is raised above earth without pillars, or raised beyond anyone's reach.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { وإلى السماء كيف رفعت } أي رفعت عن الأرض بلا عمد. وقيل: رفعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains are fixed so the earth does not shake after being spread out, as 21:31 says.
rows.anchor: فأرساها بالجبال. كما قال: وجعلنا في الأرض رواسي أن تميد بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth is spread out and extended.
rows.anchor: { وإلى الأرض كيف سطحت } أي بسطت ومدت

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: He says he heard Ali recite the verbs with final ta vowelled for first-person attribution to God, with their objects omitted; Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa and Abu al-Aliya also read this way.
rows.anchor: وقال أنس: صليت خلف علي رضي الله عنه، فقرأ «كيف خلقت» و«رفعت» و«نصبت»

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو حيوة وأبو رجاء
rows.claim: They read ‘sutiHat’ with a doubled ta and a quiescent ending; the rest keep the ta light.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبو حيوة وأبو رجاء: «سطحت» بتشديد الطاء وإسكان التاء

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: He says the order needs no special explanation; others say camels come first because Arabs know them well, rely on them extensively, and naturally look from their mounts to sky and earth while traveling.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا مما يطلب فيه نوع حكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel, sky, mountains, and earth are signs directing people to the free, powerful Creator.
rows.anchor: فأمروا بالنظر في هذه الأشياء، فإنها أدل دليل على الصانع المختار القادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to admonish and warn people; his role is that of a reminder.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { فذكر } أي فعظهم يا محمد وخوفهم. { إنما أنت مذكر } أي واعظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi first reads the verse as denying the Prophet coercive authority to kill people, then says the sword verse abrogated it.
rows.anchor: أي بمسلط عليهم فتقتلهم. ثم نسختها آية السيف

rows.speaker: هارون الأعور
rows.claim: He reads musaytir with an open ta and records the plural form; this is a Tamimi dialect.
rows.anchor: وقرأ هارون الأعور «بمسيطر» بفتح الطاء، و«المسيطرون». وهي لغة تميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Musaytir means one who controls, oversees, and records; the word derives from satr, a line of writing.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح: «المسيطر والمصيطر: المسلط على الشيء، ليشرف عليه، ويتعهد أحواله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is disconnected: rather, whoever turns away from admonition and rejects faith is the case at issue.
rows.anchor: استثناء منقطع، أي لكن من تولى عن الوعظ والتذكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greater punishment is lasting Hell; it is called greater because they were already punished in worldly life with famine, drought, captivity, and killing.
rows.anchor: وهي جهنم الدائم عذابها. وإنما قال «الأكبر» لأنهم عذبوا في الدنيا بالجوع والقحط

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: His reading adds ‘for He will punish him with the greater punishment,’ supporting the disconnected exception.
rows.anchor: ودليل هذا التأويل قراءة ابن مسعود: «إلا من تولى وكفر. فإنه يعذبه الله»

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Alternatively the exception is connected: the Prophet may fight those who turn away and disbelieve, after which God gives them the greater punishment; on this reading there is no abrogation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو استثناء متصل. والمعنى: لست بمسلط إلا على من تولى وكفر

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: After a man apostatized and did not return to Islam during three days of reconsideration, Ali executed him and recited this verse.
rows.anchor: وروي أن عليا أتي برجل ارتد، فاستتابه ثلاثة أيام، فلم يعاود الإسلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: They read ‘ala’ as an opening alert; ‘whoever’ is conditional and the response has an omitted pronoun, ‘then He will punish him.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وقتادة «ألا» على الاستفتاح والتنبيه، كقول امرىء القيس:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their return to God is their return after death; the verb āba means to return.
rows.anchor: { إن إلينا إيابهم } أي رجوعهم بعد الموت. يقال: آب يؤوب أي رجع

rows.speaker: عبيد
rows.claim: His poem contrasts the return of any absent person with the nonreturn of one absent through death.
rows.anchor: وكل ذي غيبة يؤوب وغائب الموت لا يؤوب

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: He reads iyabahum with a doubled ya; Abu Hatim rejects the reading by analogy with forms for fasting and prayer, while another view treats the forms as dialect synonyms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر «إيابهم» بالتشديد. قال أبو حاتم: لا يجوز التشديد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains the doubled reading as either a verbal noun from ayyaba or an original awab that shifts through iywab to iyab, by analogy with diwan.
rows.anchor: الزمخشري: وقرأ أبو جعفر المدني «إيابهم» بالتشديد ووجهه أن يكون فيعالا: مصدر أيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shaf means an even pair and watr means an odd single.
rows.anchor: الشفع: الاثنان، والوتر: الفرد

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Imran ibn Husayn identifies the pair and single as the prayers that include an even-numbered prayer and an odd one.
rows.anchor: عن عمران بن الحصين عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In Jabir's report, the oath refers to dawn, the ten days of sacrifice, the odd day of Arafah, and the even day of sacrifice; Ibn Abbas and Ikrima agree, and al-Nahhas prefers this as more soundly transmitted than the Imran report.
rows.anchor: وقال جابر بن عبد الله: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Ayyub's report says the pair is the day of Arafah with the day of sacrifice, while the odd is the night before sacrifice day.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي أيوب قال: سئل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن قوله تعالى: { والشفع والوتر } فقال:

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن عباس
rows.claim: They say creation is paired and God is the One; they cite the creation of people in pairs, and the account says Mujahid traced it to the Prophet through Abu Sa'id.
rows.anchor: والوتر هو الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: محمد بن سيرين ومسروق وأبو صالح وقتادة
rows.claim: They also take the pair as creation, which comprises contrasting pairs such as belief and disbelief, guidance and error, light and darkness, day and night, and humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: ونحوه قال محمد بن سيرين ومسروق وأبو صالح وقتادة، قالوا: الشفع: الخلق

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A hadith says God has ninety-nine names and is One, loving what is odd.
rows.anchor: إن لله تسعة وتسعين اسما، والله وتر يحب الوتر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another view identifies the pair as the dawn prayer and the single as the sunset prayer.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا: الشفع: صلاة الصبح» والوتر: صلاة المغرب

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس وأبو العالية
rows.claim: They take the pair and odd within the sunset prayer itself: its first two units are paired and its third is odd.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع بن أنس وأبو العالية: هي صلاة المغرب، الشفع فيها ركعتان، والوتر الثالثة

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير
rows.claim: He identifies the eleventh and twelfth Mina days as paired, and the thirteenth as odd.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الزبير: الشفع: يوما منى: الحادي عشر، والثاني عشر. والثالث عشر الوتر

rows.speaker: الضحاك وعطاء
rows.claim: They say the ten days of Dhul-Hijjah are the pair and the three Mina days are the odd.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: الشفع: عشر ذي الحجة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report makes Adam and Eve the pair, since Adam was single before being joined by Eve; another version makes God the odd.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الشفع والوتر: آدم وحواء لأن آدم كان فردا فشفع بزوجته حواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pair-and-odd interpretation may mean all creation; God may swear by His names and attributes, His acts, or created objects as signs of their wonders.
rows.anchor: وقد يقسم الله تعالى بأسمائه وصفاته لعلمه، ويقسم بأفعاله لقدرته

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: He says the pair denotes Paradise's eight levels and the odd denotes Hell's seven levels.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الحسين بن الفضل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other proposed pairs and singles are Safa and Marwa with the Kaaba, or days and nights with the Resurrection day that has no night.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الشفع: الصفا والمروة، والوتر: الكعبة

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: He distinguishes days and nights from the single day with no night, the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل ابن حيان: الشفع: الأيام والليالي، والوتر: اليوم الذي لا ليلة بعده

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: He says God is both odd and paired, citing that God is the fourth with any three who confer.
rows.anchor: ما يكون من نجوى ثلاثة إلا هو رابعهم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: He contrasts paired opposing qualities in creatures with God's unpaired attributes: might without weakness, knowledge without ignorance, life without death, and the like.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر الوراق: الشفع: تضاد أوصاف المخلوقين: العز والذل، والقدرة والعجز

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He understands the pair and odd as all numbers, since every number is one or the other, making this an oath by arithmetic.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: المراد بالشفع والوتر: العدد كله لأن العدد لا يخلو عنهما

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other identifications include Mecca and Medina as paired sanctuaries with Jerusalem as single, and paired Hajj with Umrah versus performing Hajj alone.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الشفع: مسجد مكة والمدينة، وهما الحرمان. والوتر: مسجد بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Further proposals distinguish male-female animals from inanimate things, or growing things from things that do not grow.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الشفع: الحيوان لأنه ذكر وأنثى. والوتر: الجماد

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وأصحابه والكسائي وحمزة وخلف
rows.claim: They read watr with a kasra on the waw; the rest use fatha, and both are dialect forms, though the lexicon distinguishes their senses by region.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود وأصحابه والكسائي وحمزة وخلف «والوتر» بكسر الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading leaves ‘Ad’ indefinite and treats Iram as its name or tribe in apposition; an idafa reading treats Iram as their mother or town, with an implied ‘people of Iram.’
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة «بعاد» منونا. وقرأ الحسن وأبو العالية «بعاد إرم» مضافا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings vary the hamza vowel and make the ra silent; one connects Iram to ‘those of the pillars’ or reads that God made them ruins.
rows.anchor: وقرىء «بعاد إرم ذات العماد» بإضافة «إرم» إلى «ذات العماد»

rows.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك وقتادة
rows.claim: They read Aram with an open hamza; Mujahid compares it to markers or monuments whose singular is aram.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد والضحاك وقتادة «أرم» بفتح الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse order is inverted: the oath and God's watchfulness frame ‘Have you not seen?’; seeing is intellectual, the address is to Muhammad, and the lesson is general.
rows.anchor: وهذه الرؤية رؤية القلب، والخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، والمراد عام

rows.speaker: شهر بن حوشب عن أبي هريرة
rows.claim: He reports that an Ad man could make a stone door-bolt no group of five hundred could lift and could sink his foot into the ground.
rows.anchor: إن كان الرجل من قوم عاد ليتخذ المصراع من حجارة

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: He identifies Iram as Shem son of Noah; another genealogy from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Ishaq makes Iram the father of Ad, son of Aws, son of Shem.
rows.anchor: و«إرم»: قيل هو سام بن نوح قاله ابن إسحاق

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He calls Iram a people or nation; other reports from him gloss it as ancient or strong.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: «إرم» أمة من الأمم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says Iram is a tribe of Ad; another account distinguishes the first Ad, Iram, from later descendants, explaining ‘the first Ad’ in 53:50.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هي قبيلة من عاد. وقيل: هما عادان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Via Ata, he says Ad men were enormous: the tallest reached five hundred cubits and the shortest three hundred by their own measure; another report says seventy cubits.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: كان الرجل منهم طوله خمسمائة ذراع، والقصير منهم طوله

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: He calls the reported heights false, citing the authentic report that Adam was sixty cubits tall and people have diminished since.
rows.anchor: ابن العربي: وهو باطل لأن في الصحيح:

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says a man of Ad was twelve cubits tall.
rows.anchor: وزعم قتادة: أن طول الرجل منهم اثنا عشر ذراعا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: They gloss ‘people of the pillars’ as tall people.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: «ذات العماد» ذات الطول. يقال: رجل معمد إذا كان طويلا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He also says they were pillars or leading supports of their people, meaning its chiefs.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة أيضا: كانوا عمادا لقومهم يقال: فلان عميد القوم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they lived in tents with poles and moved to seek rain and pasture before returning home.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا: قيل لهم ذلك، لأنهم كانوا ينتقلون بأبياتهم للانتجاع

rows.speaker: قيل وابن زيد
rows.claim: They say the phrase describes high buildings raised on pillars and strong construction.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: { ذات العماد } يعني إحكام البنيان بالعمد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He derives the phrase from the strength and force of pillars, supported by their boast in 41:15.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: «ذات العماد» ذات القوة والشدة، مأخوذ من قوة الأعمدة

rows.speaker: ابن الرقيات
rows.claim: His poem recalls the ancient glory of the first people and says Ad preceded Iram, illustrating the remembered lineage.
rows.anchor: مجدا تليدا بناه أولهم

rows.speaker: معمر
rows.claim: He says Iram is where Ad and Thamud gathered; tribes were traced to Iram and called Ad-Iram or Ad-Thamud.
rows.anchor: وقال معمر: «إرم»: إليه مجمع عاد وثمود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The quote that Ad boasted of unmatched strength supports interpreting the pillars as strength, with the passage cited from Fussilat.
rows.anchor: وقالوا من أشد منا قوة

rows.speaker: عوف عن خالد الربعي
rows.claim: He identifies Iram with Damascus; Ikrima and Said al-Maqburi share the view, transmitted from Malik by Ibn Wahb and Ashhab.
rows.anchor: وروى عوف عن خالد الربعي «إرم ذات العماد» قال: هي دمشق

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: He identifies Iram with Alexandria.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن كعب القرظي: هي الإسكندرية

rows.speaker: الحسن وغيره
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘its like’ most clearly refers to the tribe: no people matched Ad in strength, bodily size, or height; Ibn Masud's reading explicitly has ‘their like.’
rows.anchor: الضمير في «مثلها» يرجع إلى القبيلة. أي لم يخلق مثل القبيلة في البلاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the pronoun as the city; that reading needs an omitted phrase identifying Ad's city or its owner.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يرجع للمدينة

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: He favors identifying Iram as Damascus and describes its abundant water and produce, while saying Alexandria's lighthouse is marvelous but has parallels.
rows.anchor: واختار ابن العربي أنها دمشق، لأنه ليس في البلاد مثلها

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A report says an Alexandrian inscription identified its builder as Shaddad, who claimed no aging or death occurred in his era; Malik adds that a hundred years could pass without a funeral.
rows.anchor: أنا شداد بن عاد، الذي رفع العماد، بنيتها حين لا شيب ولا موت

rows.speaker: ثور بن زيد
rows.claim: He reports Shaddad claiming to have raised the pillars, fortified the valley, and hidden a treasure for a member of Muhammad's community to recover.
rows.anchor: أنا شداد بن عاد، وأنا رفعت العماد، وأنا الذي شددت بذراعي بطن الواد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says Shaddad ruled the world and built Iram in a desert of Aden over three hundred years; the jeweled city was destroyed by a heavenly cry as he approached.
rows.anchor: فبنى إرم في بعض صحارى عدن، في ثلاثمائة سنة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن قلابة
rows.claim: He says he found and entered the city while seeking camels; Ka'b told Muawiya that prophecy of its Muslim finder described Ibn Qilaba himself.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله بن قلابة: أنه خرج في طلب إبل له، فوقع عليها، فحمل ما قدر عليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The pronoun may instead refer to the famous pillar-built structures of Ad; another interpretation derives Iram from destruction and takes the reading to mean God ruined them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي لم يخلق مثل أبنية عاد المعروفة بالعمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamud are the people of Salih; jābū means they cut through or traversed, as in the verb for traveling through lands, and the word for a shirt pocket also derives from cutting.
rows.anchor: ثمود: هم قوم صالح. و { جابوا }: قطعوا. ومنه: فلان يجوب البلاد

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poet's lines about Ibn al-Zubayr's gift of sixty loads use jābat to mean a camel traversed a land.
rows.anchor: ما إن رأيت قلوصا قبلها حملت ستين وسقا ولا جابت به بلدا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: They say Thamud first carved mountains, figures, and marble, making 1,700 stone cities and 2.7 million stone dwellings; 15:82 also describes their rock-cut homes.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: أول من نحت الجبال والصور والرخام: ثمود

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: He identifies the valley as Wadi al-Qura.
rows.anchor: { بالواد } أي بوادي القرى قاله محمد بن إسحاق

rows.speaker: أبو نضرة
rows.claim: He reports that the Prophet passed through the valley of Thamud during Tabuk and ordered the company to hurry because it was a cursed valley.
rows.anchor: أتى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في غزاة تبوك على وادي ثمود

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Others describe the valley as a passage between mountains where Thamud carved homes, dwellings, and pools; generally it is any gap between hills that carries runoff or gives passage.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الوادي بين جبال، وكانوا ينقبون في تلك الجبال بيوتا ودورا وأحواضا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Pharaoh's ‘pegs’ mean the troops and armies that strengthened his rule.
rows.anchor: أي الجنود والعساكر والجموع والجيوش التي تشد ملكه قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Alternatively, he used stakes to torture people to death by binding them; the account includes his wife Asiya and his daughter's hairdresser.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان يعذب الناس بالأوتاد، ويشدهم بها إلى أن يموتوا تجبرا منه

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
rows.claim: He says Pharaoh raised a stone by pulleys, pegged victims with iron stakes, then dropped the stone to crush them.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن بن زيد: كانت له صخرة ترفع بالبكرات، ثم يؤخذ الإنسان فتوتد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transgressors are Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh; they rebelled beyond bounds in injustice and aggression and spread oppression and harm.
rows.anchor: يعني عادا وثمودا وفرعون «طغوا» أي تمردوا وعتوا وتجاوزوا القدر في الظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers construing ‘those who transgressed’ as an accusative phrase of censure; it can also be nominative (‘they are’) or genitive as an adjective for the named peoples.
rows.anchor: أحسن الوجوه فيه أن يكون في محل النصب على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Poured upon them a scourge of punishment’ means God sent or cast punishment onto them; sawt can mean a share of punishment or its severity, as the whip was the Arabs' harshest chastisement.
rows.anchor: { فصب عليهم ربك سوط عذاب } أي أفرغ عليهم وألقى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He says Arabs use ‘scourge of punishment’ for every kind of torment, extending the term from their own instrument of extreme punishment.
rows.anchor: وهي كلمة تقولها العرب لكل نوع من أنواع العذاب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A lexical explanation derives sawt from mixing, so the punishment penetrates flesh and blood; related words mean intermingling or mixing affairs.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه عذاب يخالط اللحم والدم من قولهم: ساطه يسوطه سوطا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: He says it means God made the whip with which He struck them into their punishment.
rows.anchor: أي جعل سوطهم الذي ضربهم به العذاب

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: He reports that Hasan would say God has many whips and took them with one of them.
rows.anchor: وعن عمرو بن عبيد: كان الحسن إذا أتى على هذه الآية قال: إن عند الله أسواطا كثيرة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says every kind of punishment God inflicts is a scourge of punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: كل شيء عذب الله تعالى به فهو سوط عذاب

rows.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة
rows.claim: God watches each person's deeds until He requites them.
rows.anchor: يرصد عمل كل إنسان حتى يجازيه به قاله الحسن وعكرمة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God waits along the servants' path and no one escapes; mursaad and mirsad can mean a road.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي على طريق العباد لا يفوته أحد. والمرصد والمرصاد: الطريق

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: He describes seven bridges over Hell, where people are questioned in sequence about faith, prayer, zakat, Ramadan fasting, pilgrimage, kinship, and finally grievances are settled reciprocally.
rows.anchor: فروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس قال: إن على جهنم سبع قناطر، يسأل الإنسان عند أول قنطرة

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: He says Hell has three bridges: one for kinship, one for trust, and one for God; Qurtubi explains the last as God's wisdom, will, and command.
rows.anchor: وقال الثوري: { لبالمرصاد } يعني جهنم عليها ثلاث قناطر: قنطرة فيها الرحم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He also glosses the phrase as God hearing and seeing; Qurtubi prefers the sense that God knows all speech, actions, secrets, and recompenses each accordingly.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا «لبالمرصاد» أي يسمع ويرى. قلت: هذا قول حسن

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: When asked where his Lord is, one Arab answered, ‘in ambush.’
rows.anchor: وعن بعض العرب أنه قيل له: أين ربك؟ فقال: بالمرصاد

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: He recited the verse before al-Mansur and directly addressed him; al-Zamakhshari praises his bold warning to a tyrant and opponents of sound belief.
rows.anchor: وعن عمرو بن عبيد أنه قرأ هذه السورة عند المنصور حتى بلغ هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human here is a disbeliever; Ibn Abbas names Utba ibn Rabi'a and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira, while others name Umayya ibn Khalaf or Ubayy ibn Khalaf.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد عتبة بن ربيعة وأبا حذيفة بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tests with wealth and bounty or with poverty and restricted provision; ‘ma’ is extra, and ‘qaddara’ means constricted his livelihood to what suffices.
rows.anchor: { إذا ما ابتلاه ربه } أي امتحنه واختبره بالنعمة. و«ما»: زائدة صلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbeliever takes abundant wealth as honor and poverty as humiliation because he denies resurrection; a believer locates honor in obedience and divine enabling toward the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وهذه صفة الكافر الذي لا يؤمن بالبعث: وإنما الكرامة عنده والهوان بكثرة الحظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers thank God when worldly provision expands, rather than treating wealth itself as proof of special status.
rows.anchor: وإن وسع عليه في الدنيا حمده وشكره

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: He reads qadara with a doubled dal; the common reading lightens it, which Qurtubi prefers because of 65:7.
rows.anchor: وقراءة العامة «فقدر» مخففة الدال. وقرأ ابن عامر مشددا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: He says the light form means to ration, whereas the doubled form means to give enough; if God had given enough, the person would not call it humiliation.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمرو: و«قدر» أي قتر. و«قدر» مشددا: هو أن يعطيه ما يكفيه

rows.speaker: أهل الحرمين وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They open the y in ‘my Lord’ in both places; the others leave it quiescent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل الحرمين وأبو عمرو «ربي» بفتح الياء في الموضعين

rows.speaker: البزي وابن محيصن ويعقوب
rows.claim: They retain the final y in ‘honored me’ and ‘humiliated me’ in both pause and continuation, treating it as a noun ending.
rows.anchor: وأثبت البزي وابن محيصن ويعقوب الياء من «أكرمن»، و«أهانن» في الحالين

rows.speaker: المدنيون
rows.claim: They retain the y in continuation but omit it when pausing, following the written codex.
rows.anchor: وأثبتها المدنيون في الوصل دون الوقف، اتباعا للمصحف

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: He permits either retaining or dropping the y in continuation because it ends a verse, and drops it at pause according to the codex spelling.
rows.anchor: وخير أبو عمرو في إثباتها في الوصل أو حذفها لأنها رأس آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining readers omit the y because it is absent in the codex at both places; the recitation should not oppose the agreed companion codex.
rows.anchor: والسنة ألا يخالف خط المصحف لأنه إجماع الصحابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘No’ rebuts the assumption that wealth signals merit and poverty disgrace: both come from God's decree.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { كلا } رد أي ليس الأمر كما يظن، فليس الغنى لفضله، ولا الفقر لهوانه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He reads kalla as saying a servant should not behave this way, but should praise God in both prosperity and poverty.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: «كلا» في هذا الموضع بمعنى لم يكن ينبغي للعبد أن يكون هكذا

rows.speaker: الله عز وجل
rows.claim: A hadith says worldly abundance does not honor those God honors, nor does scant provision dishonor those He dishonors; obedience brings honor and sin brings humiliation.
rows.anchor: كلا إني لا أكرم من أكرمت بكثرة الدنيا، ولا أهين من أهنت بقلتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They withheld orphans' inheritance and consumed it wastefully before the children could grow up.
rows.anchor: من منع اليتيم الميراث، وأكل ماله إسرافا وبدارا أن يكبروا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: They use third-person y readings for the four verbs because ‘the human’ is generic and plural in meaning; the others use direct second-person forms to rebuke the audience.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو ويعقوب «يكرمون»، و«يحضون» و«يأكلون»، و«يحبون» بالياء

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He says the passage was revealed about Qudama ibn Maz'un, an orphan cared for by Umayya ibn Khalaf.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: نزلت في قدامة بن مظعون وكان يتيما في حجر أمية بن خلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They do not urge their families to feed a needy person who comes to them.
rows.anchor: أي لا يأمرون أهليهم بإطعام مسكين يجيئهم

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: They read tahadduna with open vowels as ‘you urge one another’; its form originally has two ta letters, one omitted, and Abu Ubayd prefers it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكوفيون «ولا تحاضون» بفتح التاء والحاء والألف

rows.speaker: إبراهيم والشيزري عن الكسائي والسلمي
rows.claim: They read tahaduna with a damma on the first ta, a mutual-urging form from the root meaning to incite.
rows.anchor: وروي عن إبراهيم والشيزري عن الكسائي والسلمي «تحاضون» بضم التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turath means inheritance; its initial waw changed to ta, as in other words such as tijah, tukhma, and tuk'a.
rows.anchor: وأصله الوراث من ورثت، فأبدلوا الواو تاء كما قالوا في تجاه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He glosses ‘eating intensely’ as eating forcefully.
rows.anchor: { أكلا لما } أي شديدا قاله السدي

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: They derive lamma from gathering, so it means collecting food and eating it all together; the root means gathering scattered things.
rows.anchor: قيل: «لما»: جمعا من قولهم: لممت الطعام لما إذا أكلته جمعا

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: His verse uses the root lam for gathering a companion's shortcomings into a whole, illustrating the root's sense of collecting.
rows.anchor: ولست بمستبق أخا لا تلمه على شعث أي الرجال المهذب

rows.speaker: المرناق الطائي
rows.claim: His praise poem for Alqama ibn Sayf uses lamma for gathering or embracing, continuing the root's sense of collection.
rows.anchor: لأحبني حب الصبي ولمني لم الهدي إلى الكريم الماجد

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: He calls it forceful gathering, as in a compact stone or assembled troop; the eater gathers morsels before eating.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث: اللم الجمع الشديد ومنه حجر ملموم، وكتيبة ملمومة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He says they eat by stuffing food into their mouths.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد. يسفه سفا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He says they consume both their own share and someone else's share.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: يأكل نصيبه ونصيب غيره

rows.speaker: الحطيئة
rows.claim: His verse condemns those who mix their portion with another's, illustrating the wrongful combined consumption.
rows.anchor: يعني أنهم يجمعون في أكلهم بين نصيبهم ونصيب غيرهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He says a person who consumes his own estate then takes another's does not distinguish lawful from unlawful; idolaters also denied women and children inheritance.
rows.anchor: وكان أهل الشرك لا يورثون النساء ولا الصبيان، بل يأكلون ميراثهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: They may knowingly combine lawful and unlawful portions gathered through the deceased's oppression, or a lazy heir may squander an effortless inheritance on every luxury.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يذم الوارث الذي ظفر بالمال سهلا مهلا، من غير أن يعرق فيه جبينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They love wealth intensely, whether lawfully or unlawfully; jamm means abundant, as in plentiful water gathered in a pool or well.
rows.anchor: { وتحبون المال حبا جما } أي كثيرا، حلاله وحرامه. والجم الكثير

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: His verse uses jamm for abundant forgiveness, illustrating its sense of great quantity.
rows.anchor: إن تغفر اللهم تغفر جما وأي عبد لك لا ألما
